transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-04
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Lena Ortiz, Samir Patel (Redwood); Jared Kim, Priya Nair, Noah Liu (RiverMark)

Summary: see summary field above.

--- Transcript (timestamps approximate) ---
00:00 Speaker 1 (Lena): hey everyone, thanks for joining, um we're on for 45 minutes, lots to cover on the TTFT followup. Samir, quick status?
00:18 Speaker 2 (Samir): yeah thanks lena, so we ran three variants this week, baseline hosted gpt-like-v1 (note: model name transcribed weird), then fused-attn-v1 with int8 and a newer fused-attn-v2 path; initial TTFT numbers for 32-token inputs were 210ms baseline, 150ms with int8+fused, and 120ms with fused-v2 but caveat higher token tail latency on long sequences
00:44 Speaker 3 (Jared): wait, 120ms to first token, that's pretty solid, our SLAs are 200ms p95 for short replies, but p50 target is 100ms so still room. curious about tail behavior you mentioned
01:03 Speaker 2 (Samir): yeah so the shorter sequences look great, but when we enable streaming and larger seqs (like 512) we see prefill time spikes because of kernel selection that doesn't fuse well at long seqlen, also there's some overhead from KV cache warmup when we're switching between contexts frequently
01:28 Speaker 4 (Priya): can you explain the kernel choice, i mean what's selecting fused-v2 vs the fallback? is that runtime auto selector or a compile-time knob?
01:40 Speaker 2 (Samir): good question. runtime picks kernel by heuristics currently, factors are seqlen, batch size and hardware. fused-v2 is preferred for short seqlen < 128 on A100-like cards; for longer seqlen it sometimes falls back to a different matmul kernel which increases prefill. we can force a kernel via env flag, but it may degrade throughput for other workloads
02:05 Speaker 3 (Noah): how reliable is forcing? any memory regressions or OOM risk?
02:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): forcing a kernel is low risk for our models in staging, but int8 + fused kernels require per-layer quant params and we did see a 2-3% accuracy drift on a small eval set; probably fine for your use case but we wanted to surface it
02:30 Speaker 1 (Lena): and just to call out, Jared had sent some traces last week that showed a couple of outliers where TTFT was 800ms, Samir had a note, did you find root cause?
02:42 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes those traces mapped to two things: one, we observed a cold path where KV cache wasn't hit because the request used unique prefixes, and two, an autoscaling rebalance event that temporarily pinned requests to warmup hosts. both are fixable; caching/LSH for prefix reuse would help and we can suggest autoscaler tweaks
03:05 Speaker 4 (Priya): about caching, can we do prefix-level caching at the request router so similar prompts hit same host? we don't want to leak tenant isolation though
03:19 Speaker 2 (Samir): yep that's what smart routing does—policy-based routing by prefix hashed to the same pool for a short TTL. for RiverMark we can keep tenant isolation by hashing within customer pool. there was a transcription note earlier where our product name got munged (redwood runtime -> redbox runtime) haha sorry
03:41 Speaker 3 (Jared): lol yeah transcriptions do that. ok on streaming: we saw chunked responses where first chunk came in fast but subsequent chunks slowed, any idea?
03:55 Speaker 2 (Samir): that points to scheduling — we saw the prefill and first token generated quickly but continuous decoding was queued because of batching policy. when streaming is on we use smaller micro-batches to reduce latency but if you have bursts, scheduler packs and that adds jitter. we can tune microbatch timeout (we call it batch_wait_ms) and enable immediate flush for low-latency streams
04:20 Speaker 4 (Priya): what about sequence length distribution? our traffic is mostly 8-64 tokens with occasional long 400-600 token docs, how do we avoid long seqlen tail impacting short requests?
04:34 Speaker 2 (Samir): two approaches: rate-limit or route long requests to a different capacity pool (long-tail pool) and keep short-LLM pool optimized for fused kernels; also dynamic seqlen bucketing at the scheduler level so long ones don't delay short ones
04:51 Speaker 1 (Lena): and memory quantization strategy—are we comfortable with int8 in prod? you mentioned eval drift
05:00 Speaker 2 (Samir): depends on tolerance. int8 reduces mem and can lower TTFT a bit by improving kernel throughput, but some customers prefer int4 or bfloat16 tradeoffs. for mission-critical we recommend a staged canary and eval set to compare ROUGE/QA metrics before flip
05:18 Speaker 3 (Jared): can we get a quick sim: if we force fused-v2 + int8 only for short pool, what's p95 and p50 expected?
05:27 Speaker 2 (Samir): from staging: short pool p50 ~ 90ms p95 ~ 160ms; baseline was p50 140ms p95 240ms. numbers vary by model and infra; that's why we want to run your traces on our staging hardware to match exactly
05:45 Speaker 4 (Priya): what's the impact on cost? if we carve a dedicated short-pool are we paying for reserved capacity?
05:53 Speaker 1 (Lena): pricing note: dedicated pools are priced by reserved vGPU hours; we can propose a hybrid where short-pool is shared dedicated for your tenant during business hours and scales down otherwise — lowers unit cost vs pure reserved but gives isolation
06:12 Speaker 3 (Noah): security question, will forcing kernel flags or routing change any compliance footprint? we need to ensure audit logs capture these routing events
06:22 Speaker 2 (Samir): audit logs and kernel flags are configuration-level only; we surface changes in the control plane and log them. for Private customers we'd store those logs in your S3 or KMS-protected bucket per your retention policy
06:36 Speaker 1 (Lena): ok let's go into the recent bench artifacts Samir uploaded — can you call out the CSV numbers?
06:45 Speaker 2 (Samir): sure, there's a csv named rivermark-ttft-2027-05-03.csv in the shared folder, key rows: short-seq (<=64) 1k samples median 95ms fused-v2+int8, p95 135ms; baseline 1k samples median 145ms p95 230ms. long-seq (>=256) p95 was worse on fused-v2, about 800ms vs 640ms on fallback kernel
07:12 Speaker 4 (Priya): so fused-v2 is tradeoff, great for short, worse for long. can we auto-switch per-request so scheduler picks kernel based on declared expected response length?
07:25 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes we can add a hint header (x-expected-tokens) from client to help make that choice, it's low friction and we can implement in router now. even a coarse hint (short/long) helps
07:39 Speaker 3 (Jared): we'll probably be able to supply that from our frontend — good. any accuracy diffs on the short eval if we keep int8?
07:48 Speaker 2 (Samir): small, as i said 2-3% on our QA fail rate for a small eval. we should run your golden set to confirm
07:57 Speaker 1 (Lena): ok action items then: samir will test forced kernel in staging, jared will share three prod traces and golden set, and lena will send pricing and a short-run canary plan
08:10 Speaker 3 (Noah): timeline? we want canary next week if possible
08:14 Speaker 1 (Lena): target next tuesday for canary, so need tests by friday, that matches the next steps in metadata
08:22 Speaker 4 (Priya): small nit: when you guys said 'fused-attn' the transcript sometimes says 'fused acid' — haha
08:31 Speaker 2 (Samir): yeah auto transcriptions get weird.

-- Mid-call deeper dive (technical) --
15:00 Speaker 2 (Samir): walk-through of kernel internals: fused-attn-v2 reduces kernel launches by fusing qkv->attn->proj, which helps short sequences since it amortizes launch overhead; for long sequences memory layout causes more membound ops and the matmul tiling in fused-v2 isn't ideal, so it falls back to matmul-x kernel which is slower
15:34 Speaker 4 (Priya): are there flags to change tiling or blocksize?
15:39 Speaker 2 (Samir): yes there are compile flags and runtime knobs. we pushed a variant to staging that tweaks blocksize and improves long seqlen performance by ~10% but it regressed short-seq by 5ms; tradeoff again
16:00 Speaker 3 (Jared): could we run dual-kernel: fused for the first 128 tokens then switch? is that safe mid-generation?
16:12 Speaker 2 (Samir): switching mid-generation is tricky because of KV cache format changes; however we could route at request start based on expected output len or do a hybrid decode where we predeclare the kernel for the entire request
16:30 Speaker 1 (Lena): ok practical plan: use client hint header + short-pool with fused-v2+int8; do golden-set eval; run 1k-sample TTFT microbench; schedule canary next tuesday; monitor p50/p95 and QA metric delta
16:48 Speaker 3 (Noah): agree, also add emergency rollback plan if QA delta > 3%
17:00 Speaker 1 (Lena): perfect. any other blockers?
17:06 Speaker 4 (Priya): one ask: we need an SLA doc mapping for TTFT, not just token throughput. can you create a short doc mapping p50/p95 expectations per pool?
17:18 Speaker 1 (Lena): yes lena will send a one-pager and include canary steps and rollback.
17:24 Speaker 2 (Samir): i'll kick off the staging tests after this call and post results in the shared folder.
17:30 Speaker 3 (Jared): ok thanks everyone, talk tuesday for canary kickoff.
